summary:
Ecclesiastes opens: "These are the words of the Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem" (1:1). "The Teacher" translates the Hebrew Qoheleth — one who convenes or addresses an assembly — rendered "the Preacher" in the KJV; the Greek form, Ekklesiastes, became the English title. Tradition identifies him as Solomon, but the book never names him, and author and date are debated (the Persian loanword pardes, "parks," in 2:5 — ancestor of "paradise" — is one argument for a late date). The verdict comes at once: "Futility of futilities," says the Teacher, "futility of futilities! Everything is futile!" (1:2). "Futility" renders the Hebrew hevel, literally "vapor" or "breath"; the KJV has "vanity," the NIV "meaningless." The refrain brackets the book (1:2; 12:8), and the whole search runs "under the sun" (1:3) — where "there is nothing new under the sun" (1:9).

Chapters 1–2 run an experiment. Writing as a king, the Teacher tries pleasure, wine, building projects, wealth, and wisdom itself — "Anything my eyes desired, I did not deny myself" (2:10) — and finds it all "futile, a pursuit of the wind" (2:11). Wisdom still beats folly (2:13), yet "the wise man will die just like the fool!" (2:16). Chapter 9 widens the point — one fate for righteous and wicked alike (9:2) — and chance undoes merit: "The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong… time and chance happen to all" (9:11).

Chapter 3 opens with the poem often read at funerals: "To everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven: a time to be born and a time to die" (3:1–2). Then comes the book's dilemma: God "has also set eternity in the hearts of men, yet they cannot fathom the work that God has done from beginning to end" (3:11). Against that limit the Teacher keeps returning to one counsel (2:24; 5:18; 8:15): "Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a cheerful heart," "Enjoy life with your beloved wife" (9:7, 9) — enjoyment that "is the gift of God" (3:13). His words close with a poem on old age and death (12:1–7), "before the silver cord is snapped and the golden bowl is crushed" (12:6).

An epilogue (12:9–14) speaks about the Teacher in the third person — he "pondered, searched out, and arranged many proverbs" (12:9) — and warns: "There is no end to the making of many books, and much study wearies the body" (12:12). Whether its settled piety corrects the Teacher or completes him is debated. Its last word: "Fear God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man. For God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil" (12:13–14).
